messages.author: 7ae3dc8fc90ea191
messages.subject: riself4 format
parts:
Dear Karl, 

Could you please give me more details regarding the format of the Genotypes for the progenies / founders and the yaml configuration file in order to impute RISELF4 crossing type?

Best regards,
Guillaume.

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: riself4 format
parts:
See http://kbroman.org/qtl2/assets/vignettes/input_files.html

The files would be similar to those for diversity outbred mice; there are some sample data files at https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2data, in particular https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2data/tree/master/DO_Gatti2014

karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: riself4 format
parts:
Both the founder genotypes file and the offspring genotypes file coded in some consistent way across the two files and across all SNPs. The particular coding of genotypes and of missing values is specified in the control file. You could use 0/1/3 for missing/AA/BB or you could use -/A/B.

The DOex example (https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2data/tree/master/DOex) uses -/A/H/B. (Diversity outbreds so offspring include hets.)

karl

I guess that as the cross type is riself4, you should be able to know that 4 Alleles are needed? isn't it?

Dear Karl,

I have really appreciated your help and prompt responses.
RQTL2 works great for us and we would really like to handle not fully fixed offsprings genotypes in a riself4 cross type.
Would it be possible and do you have plan to work on such use cases?
We could contribute with our data for testing, that type of material is very common in plant breeding.

Alternatively could you point out how we could modify your code to implement it ourselves? 

Thanks a lot for your help.

Best regards,
Guillaume.

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: riself4 format
parts:
It is possible to extend R/qtl2 to handle not-fully-fixed riself4-type crosses.

The key ingredients were actually derived in the Haldane and Waddington (1931) paper; see also my 2012 Genetics paper https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.111.132647

There is a bit of algebra to be done, but it's straightforward.

How many generations of inbreeding have you done for the different lines?

karl
